name: Valley Health
blurb: Two hospitals, nine clinics and 6,000 nurses and techs. Founder Dr. Evelyn Marsh built it from the Marrow Creek rural clinic, and her family trust holds 22% of the vote.

directors.name: Oliver Brandt
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: You signed off on this system's compliance reports for nine years, and your name is on the one that missed the billing pattern. You want your name off the first page of a complaint, and you want to keep the Valley account that pays most of your firm's bills.

directors.name: Teresa Alvarado
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: You speak for 6,000 nurses, and a few of them wrote the letter nobody read. You promised them the pressure would stop, but a hospital that repays a large sum cuts shifts before it cuts executives, and contract talks open in June.

directors.name: Ruth Kessler
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 10% and your bonus is paid on year-end value, nine months away. You dislike surprises and a full repayment is a big one, but you have also seen a cover-up cost more than a repayment made today.

directors.name: Dr. Arthur Penn
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.home: Dr. Evelyn Marsh, the founder (residency classmate)
directors.motive: Evelyn Marsh was your residency classmate and gave you this board seat, and she reminded you of that last week. Her office hired the consultant, and you do not know how much she knew. Voting to put her on leave would cost you her trust, and a full disclosure would send agents to her office first.

directors.name: Imani Brooks
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You are the Chief Nursing Officer, and the nurses' letter came to your desk. You filed it, thinking a few coders were the problem, and a reporter called you Monday. You wonder whether your silence made you part of it, and you would rather say so first.

directors.name: Gloria Feng
directors.title: Audit chair
directors.motive: Your committee reviewed the coding reports the attorney signed, and the CFO told you the numbers tied out. You never tested them yourself. You want outside reviewers in before anyone says a figure aloud, because your own approval may be one of the things they find.

briefing.intro: Valley Health is a regional system of two hospitals, nine clinics and 6,000 nurses and techs, built by Dr. Evelyn Marsh, who holds 6% of the stock. Federal agents served search warrants over Medicare billing last week, no charges are filed, and the board must decide tonight what Valley tells the government.
facts: An internal audit found that pneumonia cases coded into the higher-paying group rose from 11% to 34% in three years while patients did not get sicker. Two earlier Medicare contractor reviews of about thirty charts each found nothing.

The coding guidance came from a consultant hired by Dr. Marsh's office and paid a share of the added revenue, who called it aggressive but defensible. The overpayment may be $40 million to $110 million, and no one has checked individual charts.
Valley keeps a second, internal cost report that does not match the one it filed with Medicare. Counsel says there may be legitimate reasons, and that agents will ask about the mismatch first.
Nurses sent the Chief Nursing Officer a letter saying they were pressured to code patients as sicker. It was filed, never reached the board, and a reporter called about it Monday.

Profit is about $180 million a year, so repaying $110 million would cut a year of earnings by more than half and could trip a bond covenant. Regulators have gone easier on firms that came forward first. The stock is $31, down from $36.

options.title: Disclose and repay
options.text: Report the coding pattern to Medicare now, offer to repay, and bring in outside reviewers.

options.title: Fix quietly
options.text: Change the coding guidance quietly, keep past payments as they are, and tell the government only what it asks.

options.title: Defend the coding
options.text: Keep the guidance, call it an honest reading of unclear rules, and hire a litigation team.

options.title: Reset the leadership
options.text: Put Dr. Marsh and the CFO on leave and let an interim leader decide what to disclose.

reveal.text: The real firm was Columbia/HCA, then the largest US hospital chain. Federal agents served search warrants in 1997 and the investigation spread nationwide, and CEO Rick Scott resigned within months. Settlements through 2003, including upcoding of pneumonia diagnoses, brought recoveries of about $1.7 billion.

questions: Why did pneumonia coding jump from 11% to 34%?
The nurses' letter never reached the board. Who failed?
Regulators go easier on firms that come forward. Would you repay before anyone checks the charts?
Disclose or defend? What tipped your vote?

press.headline: Valley Health Reports Its Own Billing Pattern to Medicare
press.story: The board said it will repay the difference once a sample chart review is done, with outside counsel reporting to directors. Analysts warned that a repayment near the top of the range could strain the bond covenant.

press.headline: Valley Health Rewrites Coding Rules and Says Little
press.story: Valley changed its coding guidance but told agents only what they asked for. The regional paper says the nurses' letter and a second cost report are the next questions.

press.headline: Valley Health Calls Billing Pattern an Honest Reading of Unclear Rules
press.story: The board kept its consultant, hired litigators and will cooperate only as the law requires. Lenders were relieved that no repayment is planned, but a lawyer for one of Valley's doctors is said to be talking to the agents.

press.headline: Valley Health Founder and Finance Chief Placed on Leave
press.story: An interim leader will run the system and decide what to disclose after a sixty-day review. Investors welcomed the break but asked why the government must wait two months for an answer.
